Buffalo fighting is a traditional southern Thai contest in which two bull water buffalo lock horns and push until one turns and runs, with betting central to the event. On Samui it has historically been held at small village arenas, especially around New Year and Songkran. We found no confirmed venues or dates for 2025–26, and we don't list, sell or give directions to fights. This page explains what the tradition is, what the law says and how to see Samui's culture in other ways.

People ask us about buffalo fighting because older guidebooks list it as a Samui "sight". We think visitors deserve a straight answer rather than silence: here is what it is, why it still exists, and why we have chosen not to promote it.

What buffalo fighting is

A buffalo fight, chon kwai in Thai, pairs two mature bull water buffalo of similar size in a fenced earth ring. Their owners lead them in, release them, and the animals charge and lock horns, pushing and twisting head to head. There is no matador and no weapon; the bout ends when one buffalo breaks away and runs, which can take seconds or many minutes. A bout can be stopped if an animal is injured. Fighting buffalo are bred and trained for the contest, and a champion animal is valuable to its owner and village.

Betting is the engine of the event. Spectators wager on each bout, and reports of Samui fights have described prize money and side bets running to very large sums. Similar contests with bulls (chon wua) are better known in the southern mainland provinces.

Its history on Samui

For most of its history Samui was an island of coconut plantations and fishing villages, and buffalo were working animals before machinery arrived. Fights grew out of village festivals and were traditionally held on special occasions, particularly New Year's Day and Songkran in April, with an atmosphere somewhere between a country fair and a sports day. English-language travel guides have described Samui's buffalo fights since at least the 2000s, usually as a curiosity for visitors staying over New Year.

The fights were never on a fixed public schedule. They were announced locally a few days ahead, on roadside banners and loudspeaker trucks and, more recently, in Thai-language social media groups. In researching this page in late 2026, we could not find any reliable source confirming a Samui fight, venue or date in 2025 or 2026. That doesn't prove they have stopped, but it does mean any listing you see online is likely to be out of date.

What Thai law says

Thailand's Prevention of Animal Cruelty and Provision of Animal Welfare Act B.E. 2557 (2014) makes cruelty to animals an offence, but Section 21 lists activities that are not treated as cruelty. These include local traditional contests such as cockfighting and bullfighting, provided they follow the rules set under the law. That exemption is the reason traditional animal fights continue legally in Thailand.

Gambling is a separate question. Betting on animal contests is permitted only under permits issued under Thailand's gambling laws and the Interior Ministry's rules, which in 2023 allowed animal contests such as cockfighting and bullfighting to resume after the pandemic under conditions, including welfare requirements and limits on betting. Informal betting at an unlicensed event is illegal. As a visitor, you are best off not taking part in either.

Good to know: we are not lawyers, and this is a summary, not legal advice. For official information on Thai law, use Thai government sources such as thailand.go.th.

The welfare concerns, and our position

Animal welfare organisations criticise animal fighting of all kinds. Even without weapons, fighting buffalo can suffer horn and head injuries, exhaustion and heat stress, and the animals are transported, trained and kept for a purpose that puts them in harm's way. Supporters see the contests as part of southern Thai rural culture and point out that a valuable fighting buffalo is usually well fed and cared for between fights. Both things can be true.

Our position: we respect that buffalo fighting is part of Samui's rural history, but we don't promote animal fighting or animal shows of any kind. We don't publish dates or venues, we don't sell tickets or arrange transport, and we don't use fight imagery. It is the same line we draw elsewhere: we don't sell elephant riding or chained-animal photo stops either.

Why we don't publish dates

  • No reliable information: fights are announced informally at short notice, and we couldn't verify a single 2025–26 date. Publishing old or guessed dates would send people to empty fields.
  • Welfare: listing a fight would promote it.
  • Gambling: betting is the centre of the event, and visitors can't easily tell a permitted event from an illegal one.
  • Safety: village arenas have basic fences, and frightened animals weighing several hundred kilograms sometimes break through.

Other ways to see Samui's culture

If you want local tradition rather than resort life, Samui has plenty of it, all year round:

  • Festivals: Loy Krathong on 24 November 2026, Chinese New Year on 6 February 2027 and Songkran on 13–15 April 2027. The full year is on our festival calendar.
  • Temples: Wat Plai Laem, Big Buddha and Wat Khunaram, home of a mummified monk. See temples on Koh Samui.
  • Chinese shrines: the Guan Yu shrine above Hua Thanon.
  • Fishing villages: the morning fish market in Hua Thanon, Samui's Muslim fishing community.
  • Markets: the daily Nathon and Lamai night markets; see Koh Samui night markets.
  • Muay Thai: a regulated sport between consenting athletes, six nights a week in Chaweng; see Muay Thai fight nights.
